title: Artificial intelligence for CRISPR-based biosensing: From molecular design to assay intelligence
abstract: CRISPR-based biosensors are emerging as powerful tools in precision medicine, enabling rapid and highly specific molecular detection for personalized interventions. Their performance depends on interconnected components. Guide RNA (gRNA) design and optimization improve on-target activity and reduce off-target effects, while Cas protein engineering and structure prediction reveal functional determinants for programmable modification. Meanwhile, biosensor design and signal readout strategies enable portable, quantitative, and multiplexed detection. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities to optimize these components. AI bridges molecular design and analytical performance, enhancing sensitivity, specificity, quantitative readout, and automation in CRISPR-based biosensing. This paper provides a systematic review and comparative analysis of recent progress in AI-enabled gRNA design and optimization, Cas protein engineering and structure prediction, and biosensor readout and automation for CRISPR-based biosensing. It further discusses the opportunities and challenges associated with integrating these advances into multifunctional, standardized platforms for point-of-care testing and clinical translation.

title: From affinity to kinetics: SPR as the analytical backbone of AI-driven drug discovery
abstract: AI-driven drug discovery can now propose candidates faster than experimental triage can validate. However, many models still rely on static affinity or potency endpoints such as KD, IC50, or pEC50. This reliance creates a kinetic blind spot, as pharmacological durability often depends on dissociation kinetics and residence time. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) can transform computational binding hypotheses into reusable, time-resolved learning signals. Here, we define the affinity-to-kinetics gap, link residence time to functional persistence, and analyze two AI-enabled workflows. In PRMT5 library compression, screening reduced 460,000 compounds to a single confirmed SPR binder (KD = 21.5 μM); in TNIK generative design, INS018_055 showed potent SPR affinity (KD = 4.32 nM). Across these cases, SPR functions as a quality-control filter and experimental binding validator rather than a terminal confirmation assay. We identify five requirements for AI-ready SPR data: raw sensorgram retention, consistent fitting, explicit QC labels, experimental provenance, and reusable data schemas. Treating sensorgrams, fit diagnostics, and QC labels as data infrastructure facilitates AI–SPR co-learning, providing a practical route to kinetic-aware, auditable, and reusable decision systems.

title: Data-driven computational and machine learning design of molecularly imprinted polymer sensors for phenolic contaminants
abstract: Phenolic contaminants constitute an environmentally and biologically relevant class of pollutants due to their persistence, toxicity, and widespread occurrence in industrial effluents, food systems, and aquatic ecosystems. Reliable monitoring remains analytically challenging because of structural similarity and trace-level concentrations in complex matrices. Although various analytical approaches have been developed, achieving high selectivity in complex environmental and food samples remains difficult. In this context, molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) sensors have emerged as promising recognition platforms, offering selective, robust, and chemically stable alternatives to biological receptors for phenolic detection. Despite these advantages, traditional MIP development still relies heavily on empirical optimization, limiting design predictability, binding-site homogeneity, and reproducibility. To facilitate the transition toward rational MIP design, computational chemistry and artificial intelligence (AI) enable molecular-level interrogation of template–monomer interactions, pre-polymerization assemblies, and binding-site architecture before experimental synthesis. Accordingly, this review critically examines recent advances in computationally guided MIP sensor development for phenolic contaminants, highlighting molecular docking, density functional theory (DFT), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Emphasis is placed on multiscale modeling integrating electronic structure, solvent effects, and cavity dynamics to support rational imprinting. Complementing these approaches, machine learning (ML) and AI establish nonlinear structure–performance relationships from molecular descriptors, formulation variables, and experimental data, enabling monomer prioritization, formulation optimization, binding-affinity prediction, and predictive MIP design. Current challenges, including force-field accuracy, dataset scarcity, model transferability, and reproducibility, are critically discussed. Finally, future perspectives emphasize integrated digital design pipelines, hybrid physics–ML workflows, autonomous optimization, and intelligent sensing platforms for real-time phenolic monitoring.

title: The AI-driven paradigm shift in metabolomics: Large language models, autonomous agents, and self-driving laboratories
abstract: Metabolomics provides the definitive phenotypic readout of biological systems, yet the field remains constrained by the immense complexity of chemical space, facing critical bottlenecks in data mining and the elucidation of "metabolic dark matter." As high-resolution technologies drive a shift toward high-dimensional, spatiotemporally resolved analysis, the resulting data complexity has rapidly outpaced the processing capabilities of traditional bioinformatics. To surmount these challenges, Generative Artificial Intelligence and specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) are driving a paradigm shift, elevating analytical methodologies from passive pattern recognition to proactive and deep semantic cognition. This review systematically explores how LLMs and autonomous AI agents are reshaping the entire metabolomics workflow. Under a unified “science to decision” conceptual framework, we highlight three pivotal translational pillars: (1) knowledge discovery and planning, enabling automated hypothesis generation and intelligent experimental design; (2) data-to-insight translation, focusing on spectral annotation, de novo structural prediction, and dynamic multi-omics reasoning; and (3) decision and autonomous action, integrating AI agents with robotic hardware to establish closed-loop "Self-Driving Laboratories". Finally, we critically evaluate the inherent limitations of these architectures, such as probabilistic hallucinations, physical system drift, and the "signal-to-symbol" gap. To address these challenges, we propose a strategic roadmap toward Native Mass Spectrometry Foundation Models and credible, fully autonomous AI-driven analytical chemistry.

title: AI-driven computational enhancement of mass spectrometry imaging: Detection sensitivity, spatial resolution, molecular coverage, and acquisition throughput
abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) is a powerful analytical technique that enables spatially resolved molecular profiling of tissues, providing insights into biological complexity. While advances in hardware and sample preparation improve MSI performance in sensitivity, spatial resolution, molecular coverage, and acquisition throughput, these gains are often constrained by trade-offs, where optimizing one metric compromises another. Computational strategies have emerged as a cost-effective means of alleviating these physicochemical trade-offs. Specifically, computational approaches can improve detection sensitivity and coverage by learning spectral and spatial patterns for signal detection, denoising, and recovery; achieve reported spatial enhancement factors of 2–20× through super-resolution reconstruction and multimodal fusion; expand annotation coverage by integrating chemical priors with learned spectral–spatial features; and accelerate acquisition through employing sparse sampling strategies followed by computational reconstruction, reducing the required number of measurements by up to 80%. This review critically examines recent computational advancements, with a focus on artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, while addressing ongoing challenges and proposing solutions. It can serve as a cross-disciplinary bridge by offering analytical chemists guidance on using computational tools to optimize the data acquisition and interpretation, and providing data scientists with MSI-specific context for developing targeted algorithms. We anticipate that advanced computational methods, particularly AI, will support next-generation MSI performance enhancement and enable new biological insights.

title: The evolution of aptamer discovery: From conventional SELEX to AI-driven selection and molecular engineering
abstract: Aptamers, as high-affinity recognition molecules, have benefited from recent advances in function-driven selection strategies and artificial intelligence-assisted discovery. However, the limited understanding of aptamer selection mechanisms often leads to target bias and stochastic outcomes, thereby hindering the reliable identification of high-performance aptamers. In complex biological environments, challenges related to reproducibility, stability, specificity, and translational robustness remain unresolved, while systematic investigations of critical physicochemical factors, including buffer composition and ionic conditions, are still lacking. This review systematically examines recent screening advances in aptamer selection technologies and the origins of target bias, summarizes current characterization and chemical modification strategies, and elucidates the key determinants governing affinity, selectivity, and specificity in practical applications. By integrating these aspects, this review provides a theoretical perspective for understanding aptamer performance, addressing major barriers to clinical translation, and facilitating the development of next-generation aptamer-based diagnostics and therapeutics.

title: Micro(nano)plastic detection in soils: analytical techniques, AI applications, and future challenges
abstract: Micro(nano)plastics (MNPs) threaten terrestrial ecosystems and human health, making accurate detection and quantification crucial for risk assessment and management. Herein, this review examines current methodologies for sampling, extracting, detecting, and quantifying MNPs in soils. It summarizes recent advances in soil MNP sampling and pretreatment, including key steps like collection, sieving, drying, density separation, and organic matter removal. The review compares detection technologies such as visual identification, vibrational spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry, highlighting their advantages and limitations. Special emphasis is placed on the emerging use of AI-driven methods for automated, standardized, and high-throughput MNP identification and quantification. The review also discusses current quantification strategies and identifies key research needs and opportunities in this field, aiming to guide future research on soil MNP detection and assessment. Overall, this review consolidates current advances and outlines key challenges to guide future research on soil MNP detection and assessment.

title: AI-enhanced surface functionalization in biosensors: From fundamentals to future prospects
abstract: Biosensors have become indispensable tools in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and biotechnology, with their performance critically dependent on interfacial chemistry and surface functionalization strategies. This review looks closely at recent advances in surface modification methods to enhance biosensor sensitivity and selectivity. The significant functionalization strategies addressed in this work include covalent and non-covalent immobilization procedures, along with novel nanomaterial-based enhancements that increase signal transmission and biorecognition precision. The fundamentals of surface interactions, biomolecule stability, and the shortcomings of conventional functionalization techniques are critically discussed. The primary focus is on the revolutionary effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in interfacial chemistry, where computational modelling and machine learning are transforming material design, property prediction, and biosensor optimization. The recent advancements at the convergence of AI, nanotechnology, and synthetic biology, which facilitate the development of intelligent biosensing platforms, are highlighted. A paradigm shift in biosensor development is represented by the use of AI models for functional material analysis, which provide data-driven answers to surface characterization challenges. Furthermore, the ethical issues and technical challenges related to AI-driven biosensor development are also covered, including data bias, repeatability, and sustainable production. This review systematically covers research activities during 2018–2025, providing a comprehensive overview of surface functionalization strategies, nanomaterial enhancements, and AI-driven approaches for biosensor development. Also, the review paper offers a roadmap for overcoming present constraints and opening up new possibilities in high-performance sensing technologies by combining interdisciplinary advancements in surface chemistry, nanotechnology, and AI.

title: Deep learning-driven screening of emerging contaminants: Innovations and technological advances
abstract: Emerging contaminants (ECs), characterized by diverse structures, low environmental concentrations, and complex mixture effects, challenge conventional toxicity screening. Traditional approaches face limitations in efficiency, costs, and handling large datasets. Deep learning (DL) offers a transformative tool for predicting ECs toxicity by leveraging feature learning and nonlinear modeling. DL significantly enhance prediction accuracy while reducing time and economic costs compared to conventional techniques. This review systematically examines advancements in DL applications for ECs toxicity screening in two key areas: data requirements and preprocessing, as well as innovative algorithmic architectures and optimized mechanisms. It highlights the superior performance of advanced architectures like Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Transformers in processing molecular graphs and capturing long-range dependencies. Furthermore, we analyze core technical challenges, including data scarcity, interpretability issues, and limited knowledge of environmental interactions, and suggest future directions to guide the practical application of DL in environmental risk assessment.

title: Advances and challenges in the application of artificial intelligence to medical biosensing technology: A review
abstract: In recent years, biosensing technologies have gained increasing attention for their roles in health monitoring and disease diagnosis. However, challenges such as complex background noise and signal analysis limit their broader application. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), shows strong promise to address these issues. This review overviews widely used traditional ML algorithms and deep learning models in biosensing, summarizing advances in neural network architectures and highlighting techniques such as data augmentation, fusion, and transfer learning that support model optimization for biosensing tasks. We further examine AI applications in electrochemical, colorimetric, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), and fluorescence sensing, focusing on recent progress in health monitoring, disease diagnosis, short-term glucose prediction, and virtual fluorescence staining. Finally, we discuss the challenges of integrating ML into biosensing and offer perspectives on potential solutions, aiming to provide valuable guidance for the future development of AI-driven biosensing technologies.

title: Recent advances in application of artificial intelligence algorithms in terahertz sensing techniques
abstract: Terahertz sensing techniques have been widely utilized to determine the properties of targets across a range of fields in recent years. Artificial intelligence algorithms provide a promising solution to address the escalating need for higher efficiency and accuracy. With the aid of artificial intelligence algorithms, terahertz sensing techniques can significantly improve their performance in terms of analytical sensitivity, imaging resolution, and operational efficacy. This review is devoted to the recent advances in terahertz sensing techniques assisted by artificial intelligence algorithms. First, an overview of terahertz sensing techniques and artificial intelligence algorithms is provided. Subsequently, the applications of artificial intelligence algorithms in terahertz spectroscopy, imaging, and metasensor design are elaborated in detail. Finally, a conclusion and outlook for artificial intelligence algorithms-assisted terahertz sensing techniques are presented.

title: Next-generation bioimaging in reproductive One Health: Light sheet fluorescence microscopy and AI-driven embryo metabolism analysis
abstract: Bioimaging, along with embryology is being reshaped by next-generation imaging and analytical technologies. Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM), as a leading next-generation technique, provides high-resolution, three-dimensional imaging of embryos over time, surpassing traditional methods such as confocal microscopy, widefield fluorescence microscopy, and Raman microscopy. LSFM has significantly diminished phototoxicity and enabled rapid imaging of entire embryo volumes, enhancing our ability to investigate early-to mid-embryonic development from fertilization through organogenesis in both human and animal models. In parallel with these imaging advancements, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven examination of embryo metabolism is transforming the evaluation of embryo quality and viability, as metabolic activity reflects the embryo's developmental competence and health status. This review analyzes the convergence of LSFM and AI-driven metabolic profiling as a transformative change in reproductive One Health. By integrating next-generation bioimaging into the One Health paradigm, we emphasize its potential to connect fundamental discoveries with cross-species applications in reproductive health.

title: Ultra-trace detection of antibiotic residues in infant milk formula: Advanced analytical and AI-assisted approaches
abstract: Antibiotics play a vital role in veterinary and human medicine for combating infectious diseases and maintaining animal health. In dairy farming, antimicrobials are widely used for therapeutic and preventive purposes, including dry-cow therapy and medicated milk replacers for calves. While these practices are essential for livestock welfare and economic sustainability, they may result in antibiotic residues in milk and derived products. Infants are particularly vulnerable to such residues due to rapid development, immature detoxification systems, and distinct exposure patterns. Consequently, the detection and control of antibiotic residues in infant milk formula (IMF) are of critical importance to public health. IMF is a fortified matrix rich in proteins and lipids, with added carbohydrates and minerals, which can induce stronger matrix effects and analyte–matrix interactions than regular milk. These characteristics require IMF-specific extraction and cleanup strategies, such as fat removal, protein precipitation, and chelation steps, to ensure accurate ultra-trace quantification. This review presents the first analysis of advanced analytical workflows developed over the past 10 years for the separation and quantification of antibiotic residues in IMF. Particular emphasis is placed on sample preparation approaches tailored to the complex IMF matrix and on chromatographic separation techniques, including high-performance liquid chromatography, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography, and hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography. In addition, this review highlights the growing role of chemometrics and artificial intelligence-driven platforms in enhancing data interpretation and predicting contamination risks. By integrating analytical chemistry, food safety, and computational intelligence, this review provides a timely reference for researchers, regulators, and industry professionals worldwide.

title: Next-generation point-of-care diagnostics for cervical cancer: Integrating programmable biorecognition, nanomaterials, and artificial intelligence
abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major global health challenge, particularly in low-resource settings. This review highlights next-generation point-of-care tests leveraging programmable biorecognition elements — such as aptamers, nanobodies, peptide nucleic acids, and CRISPR-Cas systems — for sensitive detection of HPV and host biomarkers. Integrated with nanomaterials, microfluidics, and smartphone-AI readouts, these biosensors enable rapid, affordable, and field-deployable screening. However, translating analytical breakthroughs into population-level impact requires overcoming critical translational barriers—including cost, tropical stability, self-sampling compatibility, and integration into fragmented health systems. We argue that future innovation must shift from performance-centric to equity-centered design, co-developed with end-users in high-burden regions. We critically assess design strategies, clinical translation potential, and implementation pathways, emphasizing equitable access aligned with the WHO's cervical cancer elimination initiative and the One Health vision.

title: Machine-learning assisted 2D field-effect transistors for intelligent biosensing and analysis
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials enable field-effect transistor (FET) with atomic-scale channels, high carrier mobility, and strongly surface-dominated conduction, offering powerful platforms for biosensing and analysis. However, translating high-dimensional yet complex electrical signals from 2D material-based FET (2D FET) into reliable analytical outputs and decisions remains challenging. Machine learning (ML) provides a principled framework to handle non-linear responses, device-to-device variability, and high-dimensional datasets arising from multichannel and time-resolved measurements. This review introduces the principles of 2D FET sensing, including material/device architectures, transduction mechanisms, and key performance metrics. The integration of ML in 2D material design, device fabrication, and signal analytics is also discussed. Recent advances in biosensing small molecules, nucleic acids, proteins, neuromorphic activities and clinically health models are summarized. Key challenges in materials processing, interface chemistry, signal analytics, and translational deployment are finally discussed, underscoring the significance of integrating ML algorithms with advanced 2D FET sensors for next-generation health-care systems.

title: Advances in deep learning for intelligent non-destructive spectral analysis: From preprocessing and data augmentation to interpretability, fusion, and transfer learning
abstract: Deep learning (DL) is driving a transition from expert-dependent chemometrics paradigm to a data-driven intelligent paradigm. This review summarizes DL progress in spectral analysis, covering the entire process from preprocessing and feature extraction to qualitative and quantitative modeling. It introduces representative DL architectures, such as convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), generative adversarial network (GAN), and Transformer. It also elaborates on the applications of these architectures to various spectroscopic techniques, such as ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy, near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, terahertz spectroscopy, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging. Furthermore, it explores critical frontier technologies such as explainable AI, multispectral fusion, and transfer learning. The discussion extends to current data-level and model-level challenges, including label scarcity, generalization limits, and deployment constraints. Finally, future research directions are proposed, highlighting the transition of spectral analysis towards an autonomous, robust, and interpretable paradigm.

title: AI and spectroscopy synergy: Revolutionizing fungal infection detection in fresh fruits for enhanced quality control
abstract: Fungal infection in fresh fruits (FIFF) causes quality and quantity loss, posing potential health risks and economic loss, respectively. Since it occurs asymptomatically in postharvest stages, its detection, quantification, and monitoring cause mistaken-prone and time-consuming visual observation and manual handling. Recent advancements in computer vision (ComV) technologies, alongside non-destructive imaging and non-imaging spectroscopic technologies, have enabled the real-time investigation of disease detection in fruits. Therefore, the synergistic integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with spectroscopic techniques is revolutionizing the quantification, characterization and detection of FIFF by rapid, non-destructive and data driven analysis. Thus, this article particularly synthesizes the recent applications of advanced spectroscopic techniques, ComV, and AI-driven (machine learning, deep learning) approaches for quantification of FIFF. Additionally, highlights how imaging and AI-driven techniques depict the strong potential for real-time detection and severity estimation of fungal contamination. These offer solutions to the limitations of traditional methods, which are often prone to error, destructive, and labor-intensive. Future research is expected to focus on integrating techniques with optimized algorithms and implementing them within assembly lines for enhanced commercial value.

title: Intelligent terahertz data analysis in agriculture: A systematic review of AI-driven approaches
abstract: Terahertz (THz) technology, renowned for its unique molecular fingerprint recognition ability and penetration properties, holds revolutionary potential in agricultural field. However, THz data analysis faces significant challenges, including high-dimensional datasets and complex feature extraction. Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as transformative tools to overcome these limitations. Unlike previous reviews on THz technology or chemometric methods in agriculture, this work systematically reviews AI-driven THz data analysis across six core agricultural domains: foreign object detection, transgenic crop recognition, variety identification, quality evaluation, component analysis, and detection of hazardous substances/pesticide residues. This review analysis reveals that AI-enhanced frameworks consistently surpass conventional methods. In optimized scenarios, deep learning-enhanced models have demonstrated accuracy levels as high as 95%-100%, marking a 12%-25% improvement over chemometric approaches. Crucially, this work highlights the AI-THz paradigm that bridges lab-grade precision with scalable farm monitoring. It provides a strategic roadmap for sustainable farming, filling a critical Agri-Tech literature gap.

title: Assessing microplastic impacts on insect behaviour through artificial intelligence tools
abstract: Behavioral analysis is pivotal for understanding insect ecological functions and stress responses. Recently, microplastics have emerged as widespread contaminants capable of inducing biologically significant behavioral alterations, even at sub-lethal levels. However, detecting these fine-scale effects remains challenging for conventional ecotoxicological methods that rely on coarse endpoints like mortality. This review synthesizes current knowledge on microplastic impacts and critiques traditional assessment limitations. Furthermore, we highlight how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping behavioral ecotoxicology through advanced bioimage analysis, including machine vision tracking and deep-learning pose estimation (e.g., DeepLabCut, SLEAP). These computational approaches function as digital biosensing tools, facilitating the ultrasensitive detection of subtle changes in movement dynamics. By integrating AI, researchers can achieve higher sensitivity and throughput, strengthening behavioral endpoints within the One Health framework. Finally, we outline future directions for applying AI to quantify microplastic-induced behavioral effects in insects.

title: Application of artificial intelligence in unveiling the adsorption of organic pollutants by microplastics in aquatic environments: Status, challenges, and perspectives
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and organic pollutants (OPs) commonly coexist in the environment. In aquatic environments, the adsorption of OPs onto MPs can increase the ecological risks associated with MP pollution. The multifaceted interactions between MPs and OPs are complex, making traditional manual analysis both time-consuming and labor-intensive. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful tools to address these challenges by rapidly processing large datasets and uncovering hidden patterns. This review focused on the transformative role of AI in advancing our understanding of MPs adsorbing OPs. We outlined the key stages in AI model development—including data collection, preprocessing, algorithm selection, and model evaluation—with the aim of improving insights into MPs–OPs interactions. Furthermore, we critically evaluated recent research progress, assessed the capacity of AI methods to unravel complex adsorption mechanisms and influencing factors, and discussed prevailing challenges. Finally, we proposed directions for future research to overcome these limitations.

title: Integration of sustainable nanotechnology with artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) for environmental applications
abstract: The technological progress over the time has enabled the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet-of-Things (IoT) with nanotechnology, making a paradigm shift in the realm of sensing and catalytic management of hazardous substances such as water contaminants, airborne particulates, and soil-based toxins. In contrast to conventional laboratory-centric analytical approaches with a resource-intensive and time-consuming nature, it is significant to develop advanced monitoring systems for real-time detection and predictive capabilities. This review explores green nanomaterials-based modern sensors and catalysts for the detection and management of hazardous substances in different environments, i.e., water, air, and soil, along with fuel generation. Life cycle assessment (LCA) approaches are significant for evaluating and guiding the development of green nanomaterials. The integration of sustainable nano-enabled sensors and catalysts with artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) systems is also deliberated. The convergence of these technologies can help in overcoming the complexities in the detection and management of pollutants occurring due to the dynamic nature of the environment. This study seeks to empower humans, stakeholders, and pollution monitoring industries through rapid sensing and predictive analysis on the basis of sensor-generated informatics using AIoT. The analysis of AIoT informatics can help in the possible risk assessment of pollutants and optimization of necessary safety measures. Finally, the real-world limitations of sustainable nanotechnology-enabled AIoT systems are discussed with significant emphasis on associated challenges and potential progress.

title: Accelerating plastic particle morphology analysis: Comparing manual, semi-automated, and machine learning-based image analysis methods
abstract: Determining plastic particle metrics, such as diameter and surface area, from soils and compost is crucial for assessing their behavior and potential impacts in terrestrial environments, yet it remains challenging due to the lack of standardized methods and the labor-intensive nature of manual image analysis. This study compares three image analysis approaches for particle characterization: manual segmentation in ImageJ, semi-automated analysis with the pliman package in R, and a machine-learning–based workflow using the trainable Weka segmentation plugin in ImageJ. A total of 926 plastic particles, extracted from organic fertilizers and ranging in Feret diameter from 0.23 to 13.9 cm, were analyzed. Manual processing required over 46 h, whereas the Weka method took approximately 2-3 h, and the pliman method was fastest, completing batch processing of all images in approximately 20 min, with an additional 1 h for manual verification. However, it correctly segmented only 42% of the particles. The Weka approach performed better, achieving 64% segmentation accuracy, though it required thorough model training. Both automated approaches correlated strongly with the manual results (R > 0.9, p < 0.001). On average, Weka slightly underestimated particle diameter (−2.1%) and overestimated area (+2.3%), while pliman overestimated area more substantially (+12.8%). This comparative assessment highlights the potential of machine-learning approaches to accelerate plastic analysis workflows while maintaining accuracy. The study supports the development of reproducible, automated pipelines by offering practical recommendations for imaging plastic particles, an open-source Weka workflow, and a model trained to characterize particles commonly found in organic fertilizers and, thus, in soils.

title: Evolution and impact of Smart Analytical Chemistry in non-destructive spectroscopy for food applications
abstract: This review critically explores the transformative evolution of Smart Analytical Chemistry (SAC) and its profound impact on the field of non-destructive spectroscopy for food analysis and safety. SAC represents a paradigm shift that integrates green, sustainable, and white analytical chemistry principles with intelligent technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), automation, and miniaturized sensing platforms. This fusion enables the development of highly efficient, portable, eco-friendly, and real-time analytical systems tailored for complex food matrices. The review systematically examines the advancements in spectroscopy-based techniques, including near-infrared (NIR), mid-infrared (MIR), Raman, UV-Vis, fluorescence, and hyperspectral imaging and their smart adaptation for detecting contaminants, assessing authenticity, monitoring nutritional profiles, and ensuring food integrity without sample destruction. By highlighting the synergistic interplay between sustainability goals and technological innovation, this review offers a forward-looking perspective on how SAC is reshaping the landscape of modern food safety, traceability, and quality assurance.

title: Empowering Traditional Chinese Medicine with artificial intelligence: Innovations in quality control, therapeutic applications, and industrialization
abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) faces critical bottlenecks in quality control and efficacy validation due to its complex matrices and subjective traditional evaluation methods. By benchmarking 116 high-impact studies (2010–2025), this review highlights a strategic transition from shallow-learning pattern recognition to cognitive knowledge reasoning, facilitated by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Explainable AI (XAI). Although deep learning architectures achieve superior accuracies (up to 100%) across modalities like HPLC and SERS, cognitive intelligence remains essential for decoding TCM's non-linear pharmacological networks. Synthesizing “medicine-food homology” with multi-modal data fusion, we elucidate a paradigm shift from empirical practices to mechanism-interpretable precision therapies. Ultimately, this work provides a technical roadmap for AIoT-driven quality-by-design, offering a systematic blueprint to harmonize international standards and accelerate the global integration of the TCM industry.

title: From passive chips to intelligent platforms: AI-enabled design, control, and signal decoding in microfluidic and paper-based analytical devices
abstract: Microfluidic technologies and paper-based analytical devices are increasingly expected to deliver laboratory-grade decisions from microliter samples, often under field conditions rather than controlled environments. This demand exposes a central bottleneck: signals are multiplexed and noisy, device-to-device variation is consequential, and manual readout cannot scale. Artificial intelligence and machine learning address these limits by linking platform design, data generation, and inference into a single development loop—the organizing principle of this review. Device architecture and materials selection are discussed alongside data-efficient optimization of channel geometry, droplet operations, and digital actuation. Scenario-specific pipelines are then synthesized for image-based readout, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy decoding, and electrochemical or impedance quantification, with emphasis placed on calibration and distribution-shift performance instead of single-cohort accuracy. Biomedical diagnostics and biological analysis are treated as demanding proving grounds, where automated readout and robustness determine whether performance translates beyond demonstration. Deployment is positioned as an upfront design requirement rather than an afterthought. Accordingly, edge-capable inference, disciplined benchmarking, dataset governance, and tamper-evident provenance are treated as practical prerequisites for translation. In combination, these elements move microdevices beyond passive hardware and toward intelligent analytical systems that deliver reproducible, decision-ready evidence.

title: A vigor signal mechanism framework guided non-destructive detection of seed vigor: Integrating spectroscopy, imaging, and artificial intelligence
abstract: Seed vigor serves as a critical determinant of crop establishment and yield stability, yet conventional vigor assessment methods remain destructive, time-consuming, and labor-intensive. In response, the field is undergoing a paradigm shift toward non-destructive detection (NDD) techniques, which integrate advanced spectroscopy, imaging modalities, and artificial intelligence (AI) for rapid and scalable evaluation. This review introduces the Vigor Signal Mechanism (VSM) model as a solution to the “black box” nature of AI-driven seed vigor predictions. This model elucidates how biochemical and structural deteriorations manifest as measurable spectral and imaging features. By mapping sensor responses to established vigor indicators, the VSM framework enhances the biological interpretability of AI models and guides the rational selection of sensing modalities. This review systematically synthesizes recent advances in spectroscopy/imaging technologies, including near-infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, terahertz sensing, multispectral imaging, hyperspectral imaging, machine vision, magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray radiography, and their confluence with AI-driven analytical frameworks for seed vigor prediction. We further underscore the inherent limitations of unimodal approaches and the crucial role of multimodal information in effectively augmenting model performance. By bridging seed physiology, sensing physics, and AI, this work provides a systematic theoretical and technical reference for the academic research of seed vigor non-destructive detection, and lays a foundation for the industrialization of high-throughput, mechanism-aware seed phenotyping systems.

title: Towards instant diagnostics: The role of ambient mass spectrometry devices in point-of-care clinical practice
abstract: Ambient mass spectrometry (AMS) enables rapid, preparation-free molecular profiling and is increasingly impacting clinical diagnostics and point-of-care (POC) testing. Advances in soft/ambient ionization (DESI, DART, paper spray, MasSpec Pen, REIMS, PESI, and related hybrid sources) broaden analyte coverage, enabling real-time detection of metabolites, lipids, proteins, pathogens, drugs, and other biomarkers directly from tissues, biofluids, and swabs. In parallel, portable and miniaturized mass spectrometers have improved the feasibility of selected bedside, intraoperative, and field workflows, particularly for targeted screening and quantification. Machine-learning integration increasingly automates spectral interpretation for tissue classification, disease diagnosis, and therapeutic drug monitoring. However, routine clinical adoption remains constrained by standardization requirements, multicenter validation, and regulatory pathways. This review summarizes the evolution of AMS and portable MS, surveys emerging clinical applications, and outlines priorities for broader implementation. We also discuss workflow integration, quality assurance, data sharing, and training needs for non-specialist users.

title: Matrix effect resolution in artificial intelligence-driven bacteria detection
abstract: Accurate detection of bacteria in complex biological, food, and environmental matrices is essential for infection control, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance, and public health decision-making. However, matrix effects arising from heterogeneous sample compositions remain a major barrier to the reliable deployment of rapid novel detection technologies. These effects can distort analytical signals, reduce reproducibility, and complicate data interpretation, particularly outside controlled laboratory settings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer new opportunities to overcome matrix-induced variability by enabling data-driven signal correction, pattern recognition, and adaptive learning across diverse sample types. In this review, we synthesized emerging strategies from the last 5 years for matrix-effect resolution in AI-assisted bacterial detection systems, including electrochemical, optical, and spectroscopic platforms. We discuss how AI models can integrate biological variability, environmental context, and sensor heterogeneity to improve robustness, analyte discrimination, and even quantitative accuracy, with emphasis on high-risk pathogens, such as those in the ESKAPE group. The workflow for AI-assisted bacterial detection is critically analyzed, beginning with pretreatment of complex samples, processing of raw data to extract the most relevant features, and then continuing with the implementation of the algorithm.

title: SERS–AI for biomedical applications: From single spectrum to multidimensional analysis
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has emerged as an important molecular sensing platform for biomedical analysis owing to its high sensitivity, chemical specificity, and label-free detection capability. When coupled with artificial intelligence (AI), SERS enables automated spectral processing, feature extraction, and pattern recognition in complex biological systems. However, most current SERS–AI studies still rely primarily on single spectrum inputs, which provide only limited information about the biochemical heterogeneity of clinical samples and may thereby constrain model robustness, interpretability, and generalizability. This review examines the development of SERS–AI from an information dimensionality perspective and highlights its conceptual evolution from single-spectrum analysis toward multidimensional information integration. We first discuss SERS enhancement mechanisms, substrate design, and AI-assisted spectral analysis, followed by a summary of representative biomedical applications of single-spectrum SERS–AI, including cancer screening, pathogen identification, disease diagnosis, pharmaceutical analysis, and therapeutic monitoring. We then discuss the transition from information-limited analysis to high-dimensional integrated diagnosis, as well as the new challenges introduced by this shift. Particular emphasis is placed on multispectral and multimodal SERS–AI strategies. Multispectral approaches, including multi-substrate, multi-excitation wavelength, and multi-biofluid, expand information dimensionality within the SERS domain, whereas multimodal approaches integrate SERS with orthogonal information from fluorescence/infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, omics, imaging, or clinical data. Furthermore, we discuss data fusion strategies, validation issues, standardization requirements, and interpretability challenges, all of which are critical for advancing the clinical translation of SERS–AI. Finally, we outline future directions for developing reliable, robust, and clinically translatable SERS–AI platforms for precision biomedical analysis.

title: Artificial intelligence-powered imaging of microfibers: Microscopy, vibrational and hyperspectral analysis
abstract: Microfibers have emerged as environmental pollutants of increasing concern because of their widespread sources, persistence, confusion with natural fibers, and ecological and health risks. Detection techniques, including microscopic imaging, vibrational spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, are important for microfiber identification, characterization, and analysis. However, complex environmental matrices and background interference still cause poor signal quality, low throughput, and limited adaptability. Artificial intelligence (AI), with strong nonlinear feature extraction and pattern recognition capabilities, offers a feasible solution. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-assisted microfiber detection, compares traditional machine-learning and deep-learning models, outlines relevant neural network architectures, and discusses strategies such as data augmentation, multimodal fusion, and transfer learning. We further review AI applications in microscopic imaging, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, focusing on identification, segmentation, counting, and polymer classification, and discuss future opportunities and challenges.

title: Advances in AI-assisted odor sensing using colorimetric sensor arrays: From sensor design to high-dimensional data intelligence
abstract: Odor sensing using colorimetric sensor arrays (CSAs) provides a rapid, low-cost, and non-destructive strategy for food safety and quality evaluation. However, practical deployment of conventional CSAs is constrained by limited stability, humidity tolerance, and reproducibility, while conventional chemometric methods often struggle with complex gas mixtures. Recent advances in nanomaterial-enabled sensor engineering have improved CSA performance, while spectroscopic and imaging approaches enable more information-rich and often high-dimensional readouts with complementary chemical and spatial information. AI offers flexible tools for high-dimensional data via feature learning, dimensionality reduction, and predictive modeling. This review provides an integrated synthesis of AI-assisted CSAs (CSAs-AI) across sensor engineering, high-dimensional readouts, AI-based modeling, and food-monitoring applications. Sensing mechanisms, fabrication strategies, spectroscopic techniques and advanced imaging methods are summarized, with emphasis on how deep learning improves qualitative and quantitative analysis of high-dimensional responses. Representative applications, current deployment bottlenecks, and future directions are also highlighted.

title: Intelligent microdevices for aquatic monitoring: High-Performance sensing integration and AI-enabled signal decoding
abstract: Water quality deterioration rarely manifests as a sudden collapse; it is more often a gradual accumulation of deviations. Changes in ion balance, trace organic matter content, or microbial dynamics are particularly difficult to detect routinely, yet they continuously create ecological stress. These signals are often too subtle for routine spot sampling or network-level surveillance, so reliable detection may occur only after regulatory or ecological thresholds have already been exceeded. Microdevice technologies are reshaping how such analytical gaps are approached. In microfluidic platforms, fluid transport, chemical reactions, and signal transduction are intrinsically co-localized, allowing rapid extraction of chemical information from minimal sample volumes with reduced latency. Microfluidic paper-based analytical devices advance this paradigm by eliminating external pumping and fixed infrastructure, relocating measurement directly to sites of concern. Integrated high-performance sensors increase both sensitivity and temporal resolution without compromising operational simplicity, even in chemically heterogeneous aquatic systems. Accordingly, microfluidic devices, paper-based platforms, and high-performance sensor hybrids are considered here as complementary—rather than competing—strategies for aquatic monitoring. Moreover, recent advances in materials science, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly expanded their analytical performance, robustness, and data interpretation capability. Device architectures, material functions, and sensing mechanisms are examined across analyte classes spanning nutrients, toxic metals, pathogens, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, emerging micropollutants, and microbial indicators. This review provides a comprehensive survey of the technologies of microdevices, their working principles, representative applications, and performance characteristics. Particular attention is given to challenges related to stability, scalability, selectivity, and real-world deployment, as well as emerging solutions. Finally, the growing role of AI in signal processing, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling is examined, and future perspectives for intelligent, autonomous water monitoring systems are proposed.

title: Application of spectroscopic techniques with machine learning for high-throughput phenotyping of seed vigor: A comprehensive review
abstract: Seed vigor is a crucial agronomic trait that strongly influences crop establishment, agricultural productivity, and global food security. Conventional detection methods are often destructive, time-consuming, and subjective, and they frequently fail to capture internal biochemical deterioration within seeds. This review first clarifies the major physiological and biochemical factors affecting seed vigor, including membrane integrity, reserve metabolism, oxidative damage, enzyme activity, moisture status, and embryo integrity. It then systematically summarizes advanced non-destructive technologies for seed vigor assessment, including near-infrared, Raman, terahertz, fluorescence, and photoacoustic spectroscopy, as well as hyperspectral imaging, X-ray imaging, and biospeckle laser techniques. Multi-spectral fusion strategies are also discussed, as they integrate complementary physical and chemical information to improve detection sensitivity and robustness. Methodologically, this review highlights the integration of spectral data with chemometrics, machine learning, and deep learning for qualitative classification and quantitative prediction of seed vigor. As data-driven models become increasingly complex, algorithm interpretability has become a key concern. Therefore, this review further analyzes how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods help address the “black box” problem, verify model reliability, and reveal links between spectral features and physiological mechanisms such as lipid peroxidation and protein denaturation. Overall, coupling molecular spectroscopy with interpretable intelligent algorithms can enhance detection accuracy, robustness, and generalization, providing technical support for high-throughput seed quality management and precision agriculture.

title: Generative AI for environmental mass spectrometry: Opportunities and challenges
abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) is one of the most powerful tools in environmental analysis due to its excellent analytical performance. Recently, the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has brought new research paradigms and efficiency revolution to environmental MS, significantly accelerating methodology development, optimizing process management, and breaking the bottleneck of complex data analysis. This review aims to introduce the advances of GenAI approaches, emphasizing their features, advantages, and limitations in environmental MS analysis. The significant applications of GenAI in sample preparation methodology and MS data process are highlighted. The opportunities and challenges for further development of GenMS are also discussed.

title: AI-driven electrochemical biosensing platforms for skin cancer: Analytical advances toward intelligent theranostic and drug-delivery systems
abstract: Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as powerful analytical platforms for the early detection and monitoring of skin cancer biomarkers owing to their high sensitivity, rapid response, miniaturization, and compatibility with point-of-care diagnostics. However, their clinical translation remains limited by biofouling, signal drift, interfacial instability, matrix interference, and poor long-term reproducibility. Beyond biomolecular recognition, biosensor performance is governed by interfacial electrochemistry, electron-transfer kinetics, mass transport, and signal transduction, which collectively determines signal generation, amplification, and analytical reliability. This review critically examines these physicochemical processes from a mechanistic and systems-level perspective. Emphasis is placed on clinically relevant biomarkers for melanoma and selected non-melanoma skin cancers, including proteins, nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, and metabolic markers, together with challenges arising from biomarker heterogeneity, low abundance, and complex biological matrices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for electrochemical data analysis is evaluated, highlighting advances in feature extraction, pattern recognition, predictive modeling, and decision support, as well as limitations related to data quality, overfitting, interpretability, and clinical generalizability. Emerging AI-assisted electrochemical theranostic systems are discussed as closed-loop platforms integrating biomarker sensing, data-driven analysis, and therapeutic actuation for personalized disease management. Finally, key barriers to clinical translation, including standardization, validation, regulatory requirements, wearable and minimally invasive sensing technologies, and skin cancer-specific therapeutic delivery, are assessed. By integrating electrochemical sensing principles, AI-driven analytics, and translational considerations, this review provides a systems-oriented framework for developing reliable, intelligent, and clinically viable electrochemical biosensing platforms for next-generation skin cancer diagnosis and theranostics.

title: Artificial intelligence-assisted Raman spectroscopy in determination of ophthalmic markers
abstract: Raman spectroscopy is an analytical tool for label-free detection of diagnosis-related biomarkers with high specificity and sensitivity, which can be attributed to the fact that Raman spectra serve as molecular fingerprints that are unique to each target molecule. However, high spectral complexity and low signal-to-noise ratios pose challenges in data interpretation for Raman spectroscopy. To overcome these challenges, artificial intelligence (AI) has been employed to facilitate Raman spectroscopy by unlocking complex information from spectral data. A typical application scenario of AI-assisted Raman spectroscopy is ophthalmic diagnosis, in which non-invasive, real-time monitoring is of great significance. This review explores recent advances, focusing primarily on literature published between 1982 and 2026, in the integration of AI algorithms and Raman spectroscopy for the diagnosis of ophthalmic diseases. First, AI algorithms (e.g., dimensionality reduction algorithms, classification algorithms) commonly used to facilitate Raman spectroscopy are briefly introduced. Then, evolution and state-of-the-art cases of Raman spectroscopy in the diagnosis of different ophthalmic diseases are addressed, including corneal disease, retinal/fundus disease, cataract, glaucoma, and dry eye disease. Additionally, limitations (e.g., safety, database unification) and outlook (e.g., diagnosis-treatment integration) of AI-assisted Raman spectroscopy are discussed. This review provides insights for applications of AI-assisted Raman spectroscopy in real-time monitoring of diagnosis-related biomarkers.

title: Convolutional neural networks in Vis–NIR chemometrics: From contradiction to conditional design
abstract: Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIR and Vis–NIR) is widely used for rapid, non-destructive analysis in food, agriculture, pharmaceutical, process analytical technology (PAT), and bioprocess-monitoring applications. Yet, deep-learning studies in NIR chemometrics often report conflicting conclusions about convolutional neural network (CNN) design: small versus large kernels, shallow versus deep architectures, raw spectra versus preprocessing, compact models versus multi-scale networks, and random-split performance versus transfer robustness. This review argues that many of these apparent contradictions arise from incomplete conditioning rather than from inherently incompatible results. CNN performance in NIR chemometrics depends on the interaction between spectral physics, dataset regime, acquisition protocol, validation design, and deployment scenario. We therefore organize the literature around three central moderators. First, NIR signals are indirect, highly collinear, and often dominated by broad overlapping bands, scattering, temperature, and matrix effects. Second, convolutional design choices should be interpreted through receptive-field reasoning: kernel size, depth, dilation, and multi-scale branches determine which wavelength spans are available to the model, whereas the effective receptive field determines which parts of that span are actually used. Third, validation design can act as a hidden hyperparameter, because random splits may favor architectures that exploit shared batch, instrument, season, or process-run structure rather than transferable chemical information. Building on these points, we propose a conditional design framework in which preprocessing, architecture, hyperparameter tuning, transfer evaluation, interpretability, and reproducibility are treated as coupled components of the modeling pipeline. The goal is not to identify a universally optimal CNN for NIR spectra, but to move CNN–NIR chemometrics toward physics-aware, shift-aware, and reproducible model comparison.

title: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy and machine learning for saliva biosensing: From substrate design to clinical diagnostics
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) technology significantly amplifies Raman signals through plasmonic enhancement mechanisms, providing unique molecular fingerprint spectra for biomedical analysis. As a non-invasive and biomarker-rich biofluid, saliva has emerged as a promising medium for disease diagnostics. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-assisted SERS strategies for saliva biosensing, with emphasis on substrate engineering, spectral analysis, and clinical diagnostic applications. Recent advances in SERS substrates, ranging from noble metal nanostructures to hybrid materials, as well as surface functionalization strategies for improving stability and specificity, are systematically reviewed. AI-assisted analytical approaches, especially machine learning (ML), have increasingly been integrated with SERS to improve spectral processing, feature extraction, disease classification, and predictive performance. Representative analytical methods, including principal component analysis (PCA), partial least squares (PLS), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), support vector machine (SVM), and deep learning (DL), are highlighted within standardized spectral analysis workflows. The synergy between SERS and ML has demonstrated exceptional performance in the diagnosis of cancers, oral and infectious diseases, pathogen identification, and illicit drug detection using salivary biomarkers. While challenges persist in substrate reproducibility, spectral standardization, and model generalization, future development of cost-effective materials, standardized databases, and interpretable algorithms positions SERS-ML systems as promising high-throughput tools for clinical diagnostics and point-of-care testing.

title: AI-driven nanostructured aptasensor engineering: Integrating biosensing, intelligent nanomedicine, and programmable therapeutics
abstract: The convergence of AI, nanotechnology, and aptamer engineering is transforming the landscape of precision biosensing and responsive therapeutics. Despite the vast theoretical diversity of oligonucleotide libraries (∼1015 variants), conventional SELEX remains constrained by experimental limitations, amplification bias, and incomplete resolution of sequence-structure-function relationships, often necessitating iterative enrichment cycles. Recent advances integrating high-throughput sequencing with machine learning have transformed aptamer discovery into a predictive, data-driven paradigm, enabling the early identification of high-affinity candidates, motif extraction, and in silico affinity optimization. Simultaneously, innovations in nanostructured platforms and surface engineering have enhanced aptamer functionality through controlled orientation, density, and stimuli-responsive interfaces, thereby facilitating ultrasensitive detection and efficient signal transduction. Beyond conventional biosensing, these developments are driving a paradigm shift toward intelligent nanomedicine. AI-driven design frameworks now enable multivariate optimization of aptamer-nanoconstruct systems, improving target specificity, pharmacokinetics, and therapeutic payload delivery. In cancer applications, aptamer-functionalized nanoplatforms enable precise tumor targeting, receptor blockade, and controlled drug release, minimizing systemic toxicity while enhancing therapeutic efficacy. Emerging DNA nanostructures further integrate molecular recognition with logic-gated activation, allowing autonomous, biomarker-triggered therapeutic responses within the tumor microenvironment. Such systems can selectively inhibit oncogenic pathways, disrupt tumor vasculature, or enhance immune-mediated clearance, representing a new generation of precision therapeutics. As a result, the integration of AI-driven selection, structural modeling, and nanoconstruct engineering is transitioning aptamer technologies from empirical tools to intelligent, adaptive systems. While challenges related to data standardization, structural resolution, and clinical translation remain, these advances establish a robust foundation for next-generation cancer diagnostics and smart therapeutics, positioning AI-guided aptamer nanoplatforms at the forefront of precision oncology.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven smart nanomaterials for pan-cancer diagnosis: A review of recent advances
abstract: The pan-cancer screening agenda is moving past single-analyte assays toward platforms that read several molecular layers from one specimen and a single measurement. Smart nanomaterials — plasmonic colloids, quantum dots, upconversion phosphors, magnetic colloids, DNA origami, and stimuli-responsive carriers — supply the physical contact with tumour-derived analytes; modern deep-learning architectures (1-D and 2-D convolutional networks, transformers, graph neural networks, self-supervised foundation models) supply the inference engine that converts raw spectra, magnetisation curves, electrochemical traces, and image stacks into a clinical readout. We searched PubMed on 25 April 2026 with a Boolean string combining cancer, nanomaterial, and machine-learning terms; the query returned 527 indexed records between January 2018 and the search date. Eighteen study–cancer entries from 12 PMID-verified primary studies were extracted with explicit AUC values and re-analysed alongside the four established cfDNA-based multi-cancer early detection (MCED) trials [1–4]. The sample-size-weighted pooled AUC across these entries is 0.886, with per-cancer values ranging from 0.840 (lung, plasma exosome SERS) to 0.999 (thyroid, serum SERS plus ResNet (Lin and et al., 2025) [5]. Fifty-two PMID-verified references span the chemistry, the algorithmic toolkit, the pan-cancer evidence base, and the regulatory framework. The pipeline that emerges — sample → smart nanoprobe → multi-channel readout → AI decoder → pan-cancer label, with a longitudinal feedback loop — is shared across solid and haematological tumours. We discuss what is in place and what still has to be built before AI-coupled smart nanomaterials become a routine component of the cancer diagnostic stack.

title: Microfluidics for particle production in drug delivery: From physical basics to perspective applications
abstract: In recent years, micro- and nanoparticles have gained interest due to their applicability to diverse biomedical fields, especially drug delivery. Typical batch methods, including solvent evaporation or homogenization, achieve high production volumes but are often characterized by low reproducibility and high polydispersity. For this reason, microfluidics has recently emerged as a promising method for producing monodisperse, finely controlled, and highly tunable carriers. Depending on the material and device geometry, a wide range of particles can be obtained, spanning from the microscale to the nanoscale and from metallic to biomimetic systems. Microfluidics can reduce waste and costs because of the limited volumes employed, while enhancing throughput through parallelization. This review provides an overview of microfluidic technologies for particle production, ranging from the underlying physical principles, including dimensionless numbers, to market applications. Particular attention is devoted to the latest device geometries and materials, as well as to the implementation of artificial intelligence and emerging autonomous formulation strategies for reducing industrial costs and development times. The strengths, limitations, and potential improvements associated with each geometry and material are critically evaluated and compared to provide a comprehensive understanding of microfluidics for drug-delivery applications. Although substantial progress is still required for microfluidics to become a leading technology for industrial particle production, owing to limitations such as device clogging, chip-material compatibility, and the cost and standardization hurdles of large-scale GMP manufacturing, an increasing number of FDA-approved drug carriers may be produced through this innovative approach in the coming years.

title: Hyperspectral imaging and machine learning for mycotoxigenic fungi and mycotoxins: surrogate detection, evidence standards and industrial deployment
abstract: Mycotoxigenic fungi and their toxins remain among the most persistent threats to global grain and food safety. By uniting spectral and spatial information in a single acquisition, hyperspectral imaging (HSI) resolves both the chemical composition and the heterogeneous distribution of contamination non-destructively and at high throughput. Taking the mycotoxigenic fungus as the central object and machine learning as the connecting thread, this review examines what the measurement actually reports, how strong the supporting evidence is, and where the technique belongs industrially. We first establish the spectroscopic basis of the infection–metabolism–toxin cascade and show that, at regulatory microgram-per-kilogram levels, the toxin contributes negligibly to the spectrum: detection is surrogate, carried by infection-induced changes in protein, starch, lipid and water. A three-tier evidence scheme is introduced and applied to characteristic wavebands, crop-matrix effects, masked toxins and the still unproven separability of toxigenic and atoxigenic strains. Tracing the methodological evolution from chemometrics to convolutional networks, transfer learning and multimodal fusion, we show how pixel-level data splitting, artificially inoculated material and incomparable metrics inflate reported performance, and we set out a validation hierarchy and minimal reporting criteria. Finally, we examine the laboratory-to-industry transition and standardization needs, positioning HSI as multispectral triage and sorting upstream of confirmatory chromatography, and identify mechanism-driven modelling, shared benchmark datasets and early warning before toxin accumulation as priority directions.

title: Deep learning integrated spectral technologies in monitoring food hazards: A review of next generation approach
abstract: Ensuring food safety increasingly depends on analytical technologies capable of rapidly identifying chemical contaminants and biological hazards across complex and heterogeneous food systems. While spectroscopy-based approaches provide rapid and non-destructive measurements, their broader adoption is often constrained by spectral complexity, matrix interference, and the difficulty of extracting meaningful information from high-dimensional datasets. Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a key enabler for overcoming these limitations, transforming spectral signals into actionable insights through automated feature learning and data-driven pattern recognition. This review positions DL as the central driver linking spectral data acquisition, feature representation, and hazard identification within modern food safety monitoring frameworks. Major spectroscopic platforms, including near-infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, are discussed from the perspective of their integration with DL models. Recent applications in detecting pesticide residues, veterinary drugs, mycotoxins, heavy metals, and foodborne pathogens are critically evaluated to illustrate how intelligent spectral analysis improves sensitivity, robustness, and adaptability under practical conditions. Beyond analytical performance, emphasis is placed on challenges that increasingly govern translation to real-world deployment, including data standardization, model interpretability, transferability across food matrices, and scalable implementation. The convergence of DL and spectroscopy is redefining food hazard detection from conventional signal measurement toward intelligent sensing systems capable of supporting rapid, automated, and decision-oriented food safety management.

title: Mechanistic modeling of flow-transport-reaction coupling in lateral flow assays: From capillary wicking to physics-AI hybrid design
abstract: Lateral flow assay (LFA) performance is governed by the coupled processes of capillary flow, mass transport, and biochemical reactions. However, these internal processes are difficult to observe directly, making LFA design and optimization heavily dependent on empirical trial-and-error. Mechanistic modeling provides a means to describe these processes quantitatively and to relate internal transport and reaction behavior to assay performance. Despite these advances, there have been no LFA simulation-related reviews in the past five years to summarize the progress. This review therefore systematically examines mechanistic modeling in LFA, from capillary wicking to coupled flow-transport-reaction processes and emerging mechanistic modeling strategies empowered by artificial intelligence (AI). We first compare saturated and unsaturated flow models, including Lucas-Washburn, Darcy-based, Richards, and two-phase models, with emphasis on their assumptions, applicability, and limitations. We then summarize multiphysics convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) models that couple flow, mass transport, and reaction kinetics to describe signal formation and support sensitivity enhancement, dynamic range expansion, and structural optimization. Building on these mechanistic foundations, we further discuss simulation data-driven machine learning, machine learning-assisted mechanistic modeling, and physics-informed machine learning as three strategies for improving prediction, optimization, and parameter inference. Alongside these advances, we discuss current challenges associated with model assumptions, parameter uncertainty, and experimental validation. By comparing these approaches within a unified model-selection framework, this review provides practical guidance for selecting models according to research objectives and dominant physical processes, and supports the transition of LFA development from empirical optimization toward predictive and mechanism-guided design.

title: Recent advances in laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) assisted by machine learning for the exploration of geochemical and environmental resources: A comprehensive review
abstract: Traditional analytical techniques have key problems such as time-consuming, low accuracy, and easy destruction of samples in mineral resources development and environmental monitoring. Therefore, it is urgent to develop efficient and rapid multi-element accurate analytical techniques. Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) technology offers the distinct advantages of rapid and remote detection, simultaneous multi-element determination, minimal sample preparation requirements, and strong field adaptability. Recently, the combination of LIBS and machine learning methods has shown broad application potential in geological resource exploration and environmental analysis. This paper systematically reviews the research progress and application status of LIBS technology combined with machine learning in the field of geological resource exploration and environmental analysis during the past six years. It mainly introduces LIBS equipment, sample preparation methods, spectral fusion technology, portable on-site and remote LIBS systems, machine learning methods in LIBS, and the application of LIBS combined with machine learning methods in the analysis of different geological and environmental materials during the last years. At the same time, it is pointed out that the current LIBS technology faces challenges such as matrix effect, and the future development direction of improving field applicability and analysis accuracy through multi-modal fusion and other methods is prospected.
